options.metric: Annual Brooklyn pedestrians injured plus pedestrians killed
options.denominator: None; count of people recorded injured or killed
options.grouping: Calendar year, stacked by injury or death
options.reason: A total count of people harmed gives a clear overview of the annual burden while keeping deaths visible as a separate severity component.
options.answer: Pedestrian casualties fell from 3,671 in 2013 to 2,874 in 2025, a decrease of about 21.7%, though the count has risen from its 2020 low.
options.interpretation: This framing answers whether the annual number of pedestrians recorded injured or killed has fallen overall, and the chart shows a lower 2025 total than in 2013 after a steep dip in 2020 and several years of recovery. It is a direct measure of recorded harm, but it leaves unanswered how risk changed per pedestrian trip or mile walked because the dataset has no pedestrian-exposure denominator.

options.reason: Fatalities are the most severe outcome and merit a dedicated trend because combining them with injuries can hide an adverse change in deaths.
options.answer: Recorded pedestrian deaths rose from 30 in 2013 to 39 in 2025, an increase of 30%, despite substantial year-to-year fluctuation.
options.interpretation: This framing answers whether the most severe pedestrian outcome improved, and its annual line shows more deaths in 2025 than in 2013 with a high of 46 in 2015. Fatality counts are directly observed but do not describe nonfatal injuries or risk per pedestrian trip, which this dataset cannot measure.

options.metric: Share of Brooklyn police-reported crashes with at least one pedestrian injured or killed
options.denominator: All Brooklyn police-reported motor vehicle crashes in the same year
options.reason: The share puts pedestrian-harm crashes in the context of the changing annual volume of all reported crashes.
options.answer: The share of reported Brooklyn crashes involving pedestrian injury or death rose from 7.4% in 2013 to 11.4% in 2025, an increase of about 3.9 percentage points.
options.interpretation: This framing answers whether pedestrian-harm crashes make up a larger share of all reported Brooklyn crashes, and the chart shows that share increasing after 2019 to 11.4% in 2025. It is a defensible crash-composition measure, but it leaves pedestrian risk per trip or mile unanswered because all crashes are not a measure of pedestrian travel exposure.
